Behavioral Design & Decision Science

Kahneman, Thaler, and the psychology of decisions — biases, heuristics, and nudge architecture.

Lesson Lectures · learn

The earlier courses assumed a tidy decider: someone who knows what they want, weighs the options, and picks the best one. Behavioral decision science is what happens when you replace that fiction with a real human being. Real people don't know their own preferences, get pushed around by the first number they see, stick with whatever's pre-checked, and reach different conclusions on Tuesday than they did on Monday — and they do all of this predictably. The single habit of this whole field is to stop asking "what's the rational choice?" and start asking "how is this choice being shaped — by the default, the anchor, the frame — and who's doing the shaping?" This lesson builds that habit from a visual illusion, a bread maker that wouldn't sell, a firefighter who never compared options, and an organ-donation form. Hover the cards, scan the diagrams, and take the quizzes as you go.

1 · The founding move: irrationality is systematic, not random

Dan Ariely opens Predictably Irrational with the most important reframe in the field. We aren't irrational the way static is random noise — we're irrational the way an optical illusion is: everyone gets fooled the same way, in the same direction, every time. That's what makes the mistakes useful — and exploitable.

"The nice thing about visual illusion is we can easily demonstrate mistakes… I've proven to you that your eyes were deceiving you. Now the interesting thing about this is when I take the lines away, it's as if you haven't learned anything."

— TED, "Are we in control of our decisions? | Dan Ariely" · in your corpus
Stop asking "what's rational?" → ask "how is this choice being shaped, and by whom?"

Cognitive illusions persist even after you know about them — which is exactly why pricing, product, and policy can rely on them. The rest of this lesson is a catalog of the most durable distortions and the discipline for designing around them.

2 · Relativity: we don't know what things are worth

The deepest of Ariely's effects is that we have almost no absolute sense of value — only relative comparisons. Drop a deliberately inferior option next to your target and the target suddenly looks like a steal. A bread-maker company learned this by accident:

"They came out with another more expensive bread maker so that they could start selling the less expensive one… This is the power of relativity. We have no idea about how much things should cost. Should a bread maker cost $49, $99, $199? Who knows?"

— FightMediocrity, "Predictably Irrational by Dan Ariely" · in your corpus

Ariely's classic lab version is the Economist subscription page: a useless middle option (print-only at the same price as print + web) exists only to make the target look like a gift. Click each bar to see how the decoy works.

"Relative to the option in the middle… the print and web at 125 looked like a fantastic deal, and as a consequence people chose it. The general idea is that we actually don't know our preferences that well."

— TED, "Are we in control of our decisions? | Dan Ariely" · in your corpus

3 · The most powerful lever in the field: the default

If relativity is the most famous effect, the default is the most powerful. Most people take whatever is pre-selected — not out of laziness so much as inertia, trust, and the sheer effort of opting out. Ariely's killer example: near-identical European neighbors show wildly different organ-donor rates, driven entirely by whether the form is opt-in or opt-out.

"The moment you set this as the default, it has a huge power on whatever people end up doing."

— TED, "Are we in control of our decisions? | Dan Ariely" · in your corpus

This is the bridge from Ariely's catalog of effects to Thaler & Sunstein's Nudge, which reframes the whole game. Don't chase one cute bias — design the environment. Pete Judo's summary runs the canonical default:

"Countries who have opt-out organ donation — in other words, by default you're donating your organs — have significantly higher rates of organ donation compared to countries where this is an opt-in decision."

— Pete Judo, "Nudge explained in less than 10 minutes" · in your corpus

Because opting out costs something — attention, a moment of decision, a tiny act of will — and most people never spend it. The default isn't a recommendation people evaluate; it's the outcome that happens when they do nothing, and doing nothing is the most common human behavior. That's why Thaler's operating rule is blunt: want a behavior → make it the default; want to prevent one → add friction. A reminder or an exhortation barely moves the needle compared to changing what happens automatically.

4 · Choice architecture: there is no neutral design

Thaler's central claim is that you can't opt out of shaping choices. Someone arranges the menu, orders the options, sets the default — and every one of those decisions tilts the outcome. He defines the unit of the field himself:

"A nudge is any small feature of the environment that attracts our attention and alters our behavior — and it does so without requiring anyone to do anything and without economic incentives."

— Richard H. Thaler, Sydney Executive Plus · in your corpus

And the reason you can't avoid being a choice architect — the bookstore has to shelve the books somehow:

"To a first approximation everything matters, so choice architecture and nudging are in some way inevitable… [critics] are living in a world that doesn't exist — a world in which there's a neutral way to do things, and there isn't."

— Richard H. Thaler, Sydney Executive Plus · in your corpus

This is also the empirical link to Cialdini's Pre-Suasion: whatever the environment makes focal at the moment of choice carries disproportionate weight. A summary of Nudge states the architect's responsibility outright:

"There is no such thing as a neutral design… the design of any situation where you have to make a choice is never neutral. It's always shaping what you do. This means that anyone who sets up that context is a choice architect."

— Fatter Wallets, "The Hidden Forces That Shape Your Choices (Nudge)" · in your corpus

Thaler's discipline — the line that keeps a nudge from becoming a trick — became his mantra running the UK's first nudge unit: "if you want people to do something, make it easy." Lower the friction on the good path; don't preach.

5 · The vocabulary — flip to learn

The exact terms the canon uses. Hover a card to reveal it.

6 · The dark twin, and the line you don't cross

Every lever in this field can be turned predatory. Thaler's own word for a nudge weaponized against the chooser is sludge — and once you see it, it's everywhere.

"Nudges have an evil twin. The authors call it sludge… It's one-click easy to sign up for a free trial, but to cancel you have to navigate a maze of hidden menus, fill out a survey, and maybe even call a number that's only open for an hour a day."

— Fatter Wallets, "The Hidden Forces That Shape Your Choices (Nudge)" · in your corpus

Ariely draws the deepest ethical line with social vs. market norms. Some relationships run on goodwill, not money — and the moment you price them, you destroy something you can't rebuild:

"Imagine I'm your neighbor and I need help with my car… now I tell you thank you and I offer you $5. That will make you angry and pissed off… I could offer you $1,000 and you will gladly help. I could ask you as a human being in need and you will also help. But as soon as I pay you $5, I've messed everything up."

— FightMediocrity, "Predictably Irrational by Dan Ariely" · in your corpus

The practitioner's test for whether your design is a nudge or sludge is Thaler's mantra in reverse: does this make it easier for people to achieve their goals, or only mine?

7 · Two correctives: noise, and the expert who doesn't deliberate

The field has two essential counterweights to "humans are biased." The first, from Noise, is that bias has an overlooked twin — random scatter. Judges hand down different sentences for identical cases; underwriters quote different premiums for the same risk. Crucially, total error² = bias² + noise² — they add, so fixing only bias leaves half the problem. The fix is decision hygiene: gather independent judgments before discussion (so the loudest voice doesn't set the anchor), use shared scales, and aggregate.

The second corrective, from Gary Klein's Sources of Power, flips the script entirely. In high-stakes, time-pressured, feedback-rich work, experts don't weigh options at all — and this is a strength, not a bias. His firefighters stunned the researchers:

"They said, 'We don't look at any comparison between options'… and they said, 'We don't make decisions,' which staggered us even more — because for them, a decision was comparing different options, and they just didn't do it."

— Lootok, "Recognition-Primed Decision Model — Gary Klein" · in your corpus

Instead they recognize a pattern from years of cases, then mentally simulate one course of action — like running a film forward:

"They were using their experience… relying on patterns they'd built up over 10, 15, 20 years… like popping a DVD into a player, doing it forward — how is this going to play out if I initiate this action?… If they like what they see, they're ready to put it into play."

— Lootok, "Recognition-Primed Decision Model — Gary Klein" · in your corpus

Klein is explicit that his program is the photo-negative of the bias literature — and James March's Primer agrees from the org side: real choices are recognition and discovered preference, not calculation. The scarce resource isn't information; it's attention.

"Historically, decision researchers look at the kinds of errors and biases that people make… My research is just the opposite. I look at our strengths. I look at the ways we can use our experience."

— Gary Klein, "Lightbulb Moment | TEDxDayton" · in your corpus

8 · The synthesis: design the environment, but know your domain

Put it together and you get a decision tree for how to decide. Click each stage in the funnel.

Worked example — a freemium pricing & trial page. You run sign-ups for a subscription product. See the forces: your current page has no anchor and a buried "most popular" tier — the environment is shaping choices by accident. Design the default: pre-select the annual plan (the one that serves the customer who'll stick around) and add a relativity-style three-tier layout where the middle tier reframes the top one as a deal — Ariely's decoy, used honestly. Make it easy, not sludgy: here's the integrity test — cancellation must be as one-click as signup, or you've crossed from nudge into sludge and bought yourself a reputation problem. Add hygiene to the decision behind it: when your team debates which tier to feature, have each person write their pick before the meeting so the loudest voice doesn't anchor the room (Noise). You designed the environment instead of leaving it to chance — and stayed on the right side of the line.

9 · Check yourself

The Economist offered print-only at the same price as print + web. Why include an option nobody picks?

It's a decoy. We judge value only by comparison, so a strictly-worse option at the same price makes the target look like free upside. Remove the decoy and the cheapest option wins instead.

Opt-out countries have far higher organ-donor rates than opt-in countries, with the same people. Why?

"The moment you set this as the default it has a huge power." Opting out costs a small act of will most people never spend — so the default, not anyone's stated preference, drives the outcome.

Klein's expert firefighters, facing a tough emergency, made decisions by:

Recognition-Primed Decision: experience produces a pattern match to a single workable option, which they simulate forward ("like popping a DVD into a player"). They don't compare — and in feedback-rich domains, that's a strength.

These effects are real, but smaller than the demos suggest

The biggest error is building a business on one cute lab effect. Many behavioral findings have shaky replication — the direction usually holds, but the size shrinks outside the lab, and over-used decoys eventually read as manipulation once customers wise up. The durable leverage isn't any single bias; it's the system of defaults and friction (choice architecture), which is why Thaler reframes the whole game away from "exploit a bias" toward "design the environment." And remember Klein's check on the noise-reduction crowd: aggressive algorithmization can flatten exactly the case-sensitive expertise that makes good fast decisions — telling real expert intuition apart from mere noise is the field's hardest unsolved problem.

One subtlety → your bridge to the rest of the shelf

Notice the throughline: in every example, the decider's own preferences weren't fixed — they were discovered, on the spot, from whatever the environment made focal. That single fact ("preferences are constructed, not retrieved," as March and Ariely both insist) is the hidden engine under marketing (you're shaping the frame, not just stating facts), negotiation (the first anchor pre-loads the deal), and leadership (the loudest voice in the room sets the noise). The deepest skill here isn't memorizing biases — it's noticing that you are always a choice architect, whether you meant to be or not, and deciding to design on purpose, on the right side of the sludge line.

Your move

Pick one real choice you design for others (a pricing page, an onboarding flow, a form, a team decision, even a family routine). On paper: (1) name the forces already shaping it — where's the anchor, the decoy, the default, the framing? (2) Change one default or add/remove one point of friction to make the good path easier — not a reminder, an actual structural change; (3) run the sludge test: is the exit as easy as the entrance? If you also make a repeated judgment (hiring, grading, pricing), add one hygiene step — have people score independently before they confer — and measure the spread. You'll almost always find a move you couldn't see while assuming everyone was rational.

Garbage can model of decision making | Organizational decision making [Game of theories #20] signal 1

In this video of Game of Theories, I’ll introduce&nbsp; garbage can model of decision making. It is a&nbsp;&nbsp; theory that explains how organizational decisions&nbsp; are made in a highly ambiguous environment. The&nbsp;&nbsp; garbage can model of decision making was first&nbsp; introduced in 1972 in the seminal article titled&nbsp;&nbsp; “A Garbage Can Model of Organizational&nbsp; Choice” by Michael Cohen, James March,&nbsp;&nbsp; and Johan Olsen. The article was published in the&nbsp; Administrative Science Quarterly. The garbage can&nbsp;&nbsp; model emerged to challenge the highly structured&nbsp; conceptualizations of organizational decision&nbsp;&nbsp; making within the traditional rational-choice&nbsp; models that dominated the management field at&nbsp;&nbsp; the beginning of the 1970s.

The traditional&nbsp; theories of decision making, management,&nbsp;&nbsp; and organization at that point took as a&nbsp; fact the existence of well-defined goals,&nbsp;&nbsp; problems, solutions, as well as a&nbsp; substantial participation of the&nbsp;&nbsp; members in organizational decision making.&nbsp; But those assumptions often do not hold. By&nbsp;&nbsp; exploring decision making in a highly&nbsp; ambiguous environment, the garbage can&nbsp;&nbsp; model made a significant contribution&nbsp; to the organizational decision theory. First, what is a garbage can in the garbage&nbsp; can model of decision making?

It is a metaphor&nbsp;&nbsp; for the chaotic and unpredictable nature of&nbsp; decision-making in organizations. A garbage&nbsp;&nbsp; can is where decision makers chaotically dump&nbsp; problems and solutions. A decision is generated&nbsp;&nbsp; from this metaphorical garbage can where problems,&nbsp; solutions, and decision makers come together in&nbsp;&nbsp; a haphazard and unexpected way, rather than&nbsp; through a rational and systematic process.&nbsp;&nbsp; Think about a trash can we have at home. It&nbsp; messy and chaotic. This is similar to how&nbsp;&nbsp; decisions are made in organizations through&nbsp; a messy, chaotic, and unpredictable process.&nbsp; A central construct of the garbage can model&nbsp; of decision making is organized anarchy,&nbsp;&nbsp; which refers to organizations or&nbsp; decision situations (also known&nbsp;&nbsp; as choice opportunities) characterized&nbsp; by high levels of ambiguity and chaos.

How do we know if an organization is an&nbsp; organized anarchy or not? We look at three areas:&nbsp;&nbsp; (1) multiple, inconsistent, and ill-defined&nbsp; preferences; (2) decision makers having limited&nbsp;&nbsp; understanding of issues under discussion;&nbsp; (3) fluid participation of decision makers. First, when decision makers have multiple,&nbsp; inconsistent, and ill-defined preferences,&nbsp;&nbsp; the goal of organizational decision&nbsp; making are ambiguous. Decision makers&nbsp;&nbsp; don’t have a coherent goal that guides&nbsp; their decision making. For example,&nbsp;&nbsp; a committee is formed to address a particular&nbsp; problem, but the members of the committee have&nbsp;&nbsp; competing priorities and agendas, and the&nbsp; meetings are unproductive.

No decision is&nbsp;&nbsp; made. The problem remains unresolved. Another&nbsp; example is that a new superintendent comes to&nbsp;&nbsp; a school district and starts an initiative he&nbsp; implemented in a different school district in&nbsp;&nbsp; the past. But the initiative is not&nbsp; well-aligned with the current school&nbsp;&nbsp; district’s goals or capabilities. The initiative&nbsp; eventually fails in the new school district. Second, decision makers have a limited&nbsp; understanding of the problems and solutions. They&nbsp;&nbsp; don’t or have only limited skills, knowledge, and&nbsp; expertise to weigh different solutions and then&nbsp;&nbsp; select the best one from a set of alternative&nbsp; solutions.

Here is an example. A department&nbsp;&nbsp; manager is approached by a consultant with a&nbsp; new solution to a problem that the department&nbsp;&nbsp; has been struggling with. The manager, who&nbsp; is facing a deadline for a different project,&nbsp;&nbsp; quickly adopts the solution without fully&nbsp; understanding it or considering other options. Third, decision makers’ participation in decision&nbsp; making is fluid. Their decisions depend on what&nbsp;&nbsp; they pay attention to at given time. Many things&nbsp; happen at once, all competing with each other for&nbsp;&nbsp; attention. This fluid participation then in&nbsp; turn, influences decision outcomes.

The fluid&nbsp;&nbsp; participation adds another layer of ambiguity&nbsp; to the decision-making process. For example,&nbsp;&nbsp; a new CEO takes over an organization and is&nbsp; driven by a strong desire to make a quick&nbsp;&nbsp; impact by introducing a new initiative. Then the&nbsp; CEO is distracted by other demands and doesn’t pay&nbsp;&nbsp; attention to oversight and accountability. The new&nbsp; initiative is ultimately abandoned one year later.&nbsp; The garbage can model of decision making suggests&nbsp; that decision-making in organizations is a chaotic&nbsp;&nbsp; and unpredictable process, with decisions often&nbsp; being made in a haphazard and ad hoc manner,&nbsp;&nbsp; rather than through a rational and systematic&nbsp; process.

To describe how decisions are made&nbsp;&nbsp; within the organized anarchies, the garbage&nbsp; can model details four independent decisions&nbsp;&nbsp; streams. The first stream are problems. They&nbsp; the issues and concerns raised by people both&nbsp;&nbsp; inside and outside of the organization and&nbsp; for many different reasons. For example,&nbsp;&nbsp; a CEO is getting a divorce and the media reports&nbsp; it. Now the board is presented with a problem:&nbsp;&nbsp; whether the CEO’s divorce will influence the stock&nbsp; price of the company or not. The second stream are&nbsp;&nbsp; solutions that are answers to the problems.&nbsp; Solutions could be ideas, policies, programs,&nbsp;&nbsp; and operating procedures.

Solutions don’t need to&nbsp; match an existing problem. Decision makers can use&nbsp;&nbsp; the solutions in the garbage can to actively seek&nbsp; out problems that the solutions may be able to&nbsp;&nbsp; solve. The third stream are decision makers. They&nbsp; are organizational members who pay attention to&nbsp; the issues with the time and energy available to&nbsp; them. Decision makers have other demands on their&nbsp;&nbsp; time. Their participation in the decision-making&nbsp; process is fluid. They may also have different&nbsp;&nbsp; preferences for different solutions. The fourth stream are choice opportunities&nbsp;&nbsp; which give the organizations opportunities to&nbsp; act in ways that can be called decisions.

The&nbsp;&nbsp; choice opportunities could be signing of&nbsp; contracts, hiring and firing employees,&nbsp;&nbsp; investing in a new company, and delegating&nbsp; tasks to different organizational members. The garbage can model considers&nbsp; problems, solutions, and decision&nbsp;&nbsp; makers as three independent streams&nbsp; that are each generated separately,&nbsp;&nbsp; and flow disconnected from each other. These three&nbsp; streams only meet when the fourth stream of choice&nbsp;&nbsp; opportunity arises. As a result, a decision&nbsp; is generated from a garbage can, depending&nbsp;&nbsp; on the speed at which the garbage is collected&nbsp; and removed from the garbage can, for example,&nbsp;&nbsp; how long before problems, solutions, and decision&nbsp; makers move on to other choice opportunities,&nbsp;&nbsp; or, depending on how long the current choice&nbsp; opportunity remains available.

For example,&nbsp;&nbsp; an unexpected crisis, such as a&nbsp; pandemic, occurs, and a decision&nbsp;&nbsp; is made in a rush without proper analysis or&nbsp; consideration of the long-term consequences. The garbage can model is fundamentally&nbsp; different from rational choice theory&nbsp;&nbsp; which assumes rational outcomes,&nbsp; consistent sets of preferences,&nbsp;&nbsp; knowledge of alternative solutions, and&nbsp; a full capacity of the decision makers to&nbsp;&nbsp; calculate the probabilities of success of each&nbsp; course of action. But organizational decisions&nbsp;&nbsp; are usually not made in such a linear,&nbsp; coherent, rational, and predictable way.

According to the garbage can model of&nbsp; decision making, the four streams are&nbsp;&nbsp; unrelated or only loosely coupled most of the&nbsp; time. They converge only when they happen to&nbsp;&nbsp; be simultaneously available at a specific point&nbsp; in time. This is because problems and solutions&nbsp;&nbsp; are thrown into the garbage can and become&nbsp; connected with each other by chance. This&nbsp;&nbsp; makes decision-making process a result of random&nbsp; encounters, instead of a rational process. The&nbsp;&nbsp; decision-making process can be chaotic. Solutions&nbsp; could be proposed when there is no clear problem&nbsp;&nbsp; present.

Decisions are sometimes made without&nbsp; any problems being solved. Other times,&nbsp;&nbsp; decisions are not made. Still other times,&nbsp; decisions are made, but do not address the&nbsp;&nbsp; problem that they were meant to solve. And those&nbsp; problems could persist without being solved. The garbage can model of decision making&nbsp; explains the seemingly fortuitous and&nbsp;&nbsp; contradictory behavior in organizational decision&nbsp; making. It treats organizational decision making&nbsp;&nbsp; as a collective phenomenon, not an individual&nbsp; decision maker’s mental process. In doing so,&nbsp;&nbsp; the garbage can model adds extra complexity&nbsp; to organizational decision making by shifting&nbsp;&nbsp; decision-making processes from an&nbsp; individual process to a more macro,&nbsp;&nbsp; aggregated, organizational-level decision making.

After the garbage can model was proposed, it was&nbsp; criticized for amplifying the “anarchic” nature&nbsp;&nbsp; of decision making. A few years later,&nbsp; neo-institutional theory was proposed&nbsp;&nbsp; and complemented the garbage can model by&nbsp; describing how decision making may occur&nbsp;&nbsp; in a more organized manner. Regardless, a purely&nbsp; rational view is not the best theory to explain&nbsp;&nbsp; organizational decision making. How the garbage&nbsp; can model of decision making was generated was&nbsp;&nbsp; actually a testament of the model itself. In&nbsp; 1968, Johan Olsen was a doctoral student in&nbsp;&nbsp; Norway and went to the University of California,&nbsp; Irvine as a visiting scholar.

At that time,&nbsp;&nbsp; James March was both the Dean of the School of&nbsp; Social Sciences and a professor of psychology&nbsp;&nbsp; and sociology at the University of California,&nbsp; Irvine. Meanwhile, Michael Cohen was a doctoral&nbsp;&nbsp; student who was just beginning his work&nbsp; as a research assistant to James March.&nbsp;&nbsp; Since it was the last year for James March to&nbsp; serve as dean, the university conducted a search&nbsp;&nbsp; process to hire a new dean. But the search process&nbsp; ended with none of the potential candidates being&nbsp;&nbsp; chosen. And the head of the search committee&nbsp; ended up taking the position of dean.

Johan Olsen observed the chaotic decision-making&nbsp; process throughout the search process. The topics&nbsp;&nbsp; that were previously considered to be&nbsp; important to the decision making process,&nbsp;&nbsp; became less important, and were instead trumped&nbsp; by issues such as time constraints of the search&nbsp;&nbsp; committee members. For example, one search&nbsp; committee member was present in one meeting,&nbsp;&nbsp; but was absent from the following&nbsp; meeting due to professional travel&nbsp;&nbsp; commitments. Johan Olsen also observed that&nbsp; committee members gave each other head nods,&nbsp;&nbsp; and other non-verbal communication, in meetings,&nbsp; and thought about the possible communication,&nbsp;&nbsp; or miscommunication.

The silence of the current&nbsp; dean, who was James March, could be misinterpreted&nbsp;&nbsp; by the search committee that candidates&nbsp; did not have the current dean’s support. By 1972, three authors had all moved&nbsp; from the University of California,&nbsp;&nbsp; Irvine to Stanford University. James&nbsp; March took the position of professor.&nbsp;&nbsp; Michael Cohen was post-doctoral fellow,&nbsp; and Johan Olsen a visiting professor.&nbsp;&nbsp; They worked together to develop the garbage&nbsp; can model and published the paper “A Garbage&nbsp;&nbsp; Can Model of Organizational Choice.” They later&nbsp; published more work on the garbage can model,&nbsp;&nbsp; such as "The Garbage Can Model of&nbsp; Organizational Choice: A reply to&nbsp;&nbsp; Critics" in 1982 and "The Garbage Can Model of&nbsp; Organizational Choice: An assessment" in 1995.

As researchers, how can we refine or challenge&nbsp; the garbage can model? Here are some ideas.&nbsp; How does artificial intelligence influence&nbsp; organizational decision-making process? Does&nbsp;&nbsp; the garbage can model still apply when&nbsp; many decisions are made by algorithms?&nbsp; How does the garbage can model apply&nbsp; to different types of organizations,&nbsp;&nbsp; such as non-profit organizations,&nbsp; government agencies, and small businesses?&nbsp; How does the garbage can model work over&nbsp; time? Can we add another stream of time&nbsp;&nbsp; to the model? If so, how does it work?

So if I were struggling with meeting my artificial deadlines, imagine how effective it would be setting up a $500 punishment, where if I don't have a video rendering in my computer before I go to sleep, I have to pay $500 to a charity that I absolutely hate. Well I can guarantee you, I would do anything and always have it ready just so that wouldn't happen. And there are so many aspects to procrastination, which I will probably address at some point in maybe a quote unquote ultimate guide to it or whatever, but this particular part is a huge part. So again, One... Set up artificial deadlines. Two...

If you're not meeting them, set up some really unpleasant punishments, and I will guarantee you that you will meet them. I had a friend a few years ago who had major trouble approaching girls that he liked. Pre-Suasion by Robert Cialdini - Summary & Review (ANIMATED) signal 1
Successful By Design · 12:34 · 153,100 views · Watch ↗
Read transcript · ~1,669 words

Robert Cialdini is one of the world's leading experts in the field of influence psychology. His fascinating book "Influence" came out 35 years ago, but it is still on the bookshelves of the most influential and successful people in the world. And while Influence deals with "persuasion," the art and science of getting someone to say "YES," Cialdini's new book is about PRE-persuasion: the process of organizing recipients to be receptive to a message BEFORE they encounter it. It is essentially the psychological framework in which you deliver your message. And that framework matters. A lot. Cialdini spent years studying the best salespeople, marketers, negotiators, and public speakers, and what he noticed was that the best performers spent more time crafting what they do and say before making a request than on the request itself.

PRE-suasion offers a set of very practical ways to make people more receptive to your message, request, or proposal even before you deliver it to them. Just consider this example from the book: a consultant friend of the author was having trouble with prospects asking for discounts and challenging his rates when he was doing his pitch. One day, the consultant finished the joke, "As you can see, I'm not going to be able to charge you a million dollars for this," before stating his price. After this casual joke, no one challenged his $75,000 consulting fee. So, he made it a permanent part of his sales presentation and was never challenged again.

What he found, by chance, was the powerful concept of "price anchoring". Mentioning a million dollars, even as a joke, made his $75,000 fee seem insignificant in comparison. By bringing forward his perspectives, he practically eliminated a major objection. How can YOU use these powerful tactics? 1) Attention When you pay attention to something, it will automatically become more important to you, or at least it will seem that way. The mainstream media take advantage of that on a daily basis. Experts believe that the media does not directly change people's opinions. But what they can do is change which story or topic receives more attention.

They control what is being said. And when something or someone gets a lot of coverage, people assume it's important. The lesson here is: attention = importance. If you want to persuade someone of anything, you need to be able to capture, hold, and direct their attention. Cialdini offers 4 tactics that can transform you into a master of attention: 1) How to change the direction of someone's attention. In the most trivial argument you may have at work or at home, you are trying to convince someone by giving them reasons. But that's typically the hardest way to change someone's mind... as we've all experienced.

A much easier and more powerful tactic is to change what that person is paying attention to. Since attention is limited and you can usually only focus on one thing at a time, when something new comes up, you almost immediately abandon the old thing. You can see this tactic in use by many politicians. When asked about the negative impact of a construction project, for example, they almost never argue, but change the narrative by talking about the new jobs created or the economic effect it will have on the neighborhood. By shifting the focus, they can also change the way people view the given project. 2) How to ask the "right" questions Using specific questions is a powerful way to direct attention to where it is needed.

In a Canadian study, people were asked one of two questions: Are you "happy" with your social life or are you "unhappy" with your social life? Although the questions may seem identical to most, the results are nothing short of surprising. People who were asked if they were unhappy were 375% more likely to say yes. The way the question was phrased made some people think about their happiness and others about their unhappiness, hence the big difference in the results. REMEMBER: Questions are an extremely powerful way to guide someone's attention. 3) How to get attention Before you can direct someone's attention, you must first be able to capture it.

How do you do that? Using time-tested attention testers: SEX The main reason you see models on magazine covers and in advertisements. Attractive people make you notice things, and while you're looking, you also notice the headlines, the products, and everything else. DANGER: a tactic similar to sex, but with the opposite message. Dangers and threats are attention magnets that the health industry is making very powerful use of. NOVELTY: For something to be noticed, it must stand out, be different, be new. If you're going to receive junk mail in a bright pink envelope, chances are you'll open it (at least the first time).

In the sea of ​​letters, while, it will stand out demanding your attention. Once you have captured that valuable attention, how can you retain it? By using the most interesting person in the world for each person: themselves. Talking about the other person using "YOU" instead of "people" or "they" will make them pay attention. Or, speaking of its qualities and characteristics. That's why you hear many commercials using language like "in your 40s and overweight" or "you're a 50-year-old man struggling to find X." Make the other person the topic of conversation, and they'll pay attention to it almost indefinitely.

So far you've become a master of attention, what's the next step in pre-persuasion? Cialdini calls for "unity". The feeling of being part of something bigger than yourself. It can be a shared group, a shared identity, or even a shared worldview. When a sports team wins or loses, its fans don't say "the team lost" or "they lost," they usually say "we lost." Similarly, religious people tend to refer to their churches as "our church". And, of course, the greatest unit of all: a family. There is nothing more united than a family, and that is why there are so many advertisements cleverly using language associated with family.

The lesson here is to use language and actions to make people feel that they are part of something bigger, and that you are one of them. Invoke unity and you can influence them more powerfully. The final part of pre-persuasion is "connections". If you can design new or different mention connections, you can influence people more easily. Almost all large companies use this powerful tactic as part of their branding. That's why when you think of Mercedes Benz, you think of luxury, and when you think of Wal-Mart, you think of convenience and low prices. These associations have been carefully created by forging connections in your mind.

This is usually done by showing them a scenario of some kind, or an attractive model or a well-known celebrity, and then linking the product or company simply by showing it. Just look at the next advertisement you see and you will notice nothing more than a background and a product image that often have nothing to do with each other, but create a powerful and subtle connection in your mind. Connections are also formed by being specific with the language and the words you use. Presenting something as an investment will have a connection versus presenting the cost of the exact same thing. And finally, use connections to build self-confidence.

Cialdini followed a successful home alarm salesman. In the middle of his home presentation, he hit his forehead and said yes. I forgot something important in the car. Then he would ask the million-dollar question: "I don't want to interrupt your presentation, do you mind if I step outside and come back inside your house?" It's extremely subtle, but when you break it down, it's very powerful. Who do you let come and go from your house on their own? Only someone you trust, of course, a close friend or a family member. By evoking that mental connection, the salesperson was becoming much more trustworthy and, as a result, it was easier to close the sale.

Let's sum it all up: the next time you want to persuade someone to keep these 3 things in mind: Attention: where is it going and can they hold it? Unit: Are you part of the team or are you part of them? Can you prove that? Connections: What positive mental connections and associations are you making? Now, let's see how you can make use of all these powerful tactics in your life.

The Hidden Forces That Shape Your Choices (Nudge by Richard Thaler & Cass Sunstein)
Fatter Wallets · 6:29 · 2 views · Watch ↗
Read transcript · ~1,321 words

Welcome to Fatter Wallet's book summaries. Today we're diving into a book that I promise you is going to completely change the way you look at every single choice you make. The book is Nudge by Richard Thaylor and Cass Sunstein. And it's all about how these small subtle pushes can guide us toward making way better decisions about our health, our happiness, and especially our money. All right, let's be real for a second. Have you ever done this? You sign up for some free trial and then like 5 years down the line you realize you're still paying for it even though you haven't touched it in ages. Yeah, you are not alone.

And there's a fascinating reason why we all fall into that trap. So this gets right to the core problem the book tackles. Traditional economics assumes we're all these perfectly rational creatures called eons. But in the real world, well, we're just humans. You see, these econ from the textbooks are basically superheroes. They think like Einstein. They have the willpower of Gandhi. They never make a bad call. But then there's us, actual humans. You know, we have trouble with long division sometimes. We forget important birthdays. And yes, we get hangovers. The point is, we make mistakes and importantly, we make them in very predictable ways.

And we're not just talking about small slip ups here. The consequences of our humanness can be huge. For instance, over 40% of adults in the US are considered obese. Now, that's not a judgment. It's a statistic that shows what happens when we consistently make choices that feel good in the moment, but aren't great for us in the long run. So, why do we do this to ourselves? Well, Nudge explains it using a brilliant framework that's all about the two competing systems inside our brain. Think of it like having two different operating systems running at the same time. Okay, let's try a quick puzzle straight from the book.

Ready? A bat and a ball together cost $110. The bat costs exactly $1 more than the ball. So, how much does the ball cost? Just go with your first gut instinct. What's the number that just popped into your head? If you're like pretty much everyone else, you immediately thought 10 cents. It just feels right, doesn't it? That feeling, that instant answer, that's your automatic system at work. It's fast, it's intuitive, and it's often wrong. The correct answer is actually 5. See, if the ball is 5, the bat is $15, which adds up to 110. To get there, you had to stop, engage your brain, and do the actual math.

That's your other system, the slow, logical, reflective system. Basically, our automatic system is like Homer Simpson, and our reflective system is like Mr. Spock. Okay? So, if we know we're flawed humans who rely too much on our inner Homer Simpson, what's the solution? This is where the book's biggest idea comes into play, something called choice architecture. And the core insight is this. There is no such thing as a neutral design. Think about it. When an architect designs a building, where they put the staircases or the cafeteria influences how people interact. In the same way, the design of any situation where you have to make a choice is never neutral.

It's always shaping what you do. This means that anyone who sets up that context is a choice architect. And that's not just some fancy designer. It's the doctor who explains your treatment options, the manager who created your company's retirement plan form, or even a parent who arranges the food in the fridge. A lot of us are choice architects, and we don't even know it. And the main tool of a choice architect is the nudge. It's any little detail in the environment that influences our choice. Now, here's the crucial part. A nudge doesn't ban anything or force your hand. So, putting fruit at eye level in a cafeteria is a nudge.

Banning junk food is not. It's all about making the better choice the easier choice. So, how does all this tie back to our finances? Well, our wallets are pretty much ground zero for nudges. Because when it comes to money, our brains are full of these predictable biases. The book lists a ton of these, but let's just look at a few of the big ones. We've got status quo bias, which is our tendency to just stick with the default option. There's lost aversion, which means we hate losing something more than we like goning the exact same thing. And then there's framing, which is all about how a choice is presented.

Here's a perfect example of loss aversion. If a store offers you a 5-cent discount for bringing a reusable bag, it has almost no effect. But if that same store charges you a 5-cent fee for taking a plastic one, usage drops dramatically. We will work way harder to avoid a tiny loss than we will to get a tiny gain. And check out framing in action. If a doctor tells you that out of 100 patients 90 are alive after 5 years, you feel pretty good, right? But what if they say out of 100 patients 10 are dead after 5 years? It sounds so much scarier. It's the exact same information, but the way it's framed completely changes how you feel about it.

Now, you better believe companies know all about this stuff. The book uses the Cinnabon example. You're walking through the airport, your logical, reflective brain says, "Maybe I should get a yogurt." But then Cinnabon intentionally pumps that irresistible smell right into your path. They are directly targeting your automatic Homer Simpson brain. And we all know which line is usually longer. So, while nudges can be used for good, they have an evil twin. The authors call it sludge. This is when choice architects intentionally add friction to make it harder for you to do something that's in your best interest but not necessarily theirs.

And we have all been victims of sludge. Think about how it's oneclick easy to sign up for a free trial, but to cancel you have to navigate a maze of hidden menus, fill out a survey, and maybe even call a number that's only open for an hour a day. That, my friends, is pure sludge. So, if you take away just one big idea from all this, let it be this one. These tiny, seemingly insignificant details in how choices are presented to us can lead to absolutely massive changes in our behavior. They aren't just details. They can steer millions of people towards better outcomes. So, the big question the book leaves you with is this.

Now that you have the language for this nudges, sludge, choice architecture, where do you see it? Start looking around. at the grocery store, on the websites you browse, in your workplace, because once you start seeing it, you can't unsee it. Fatter wallets
